Schools and movements

Embodied cognition

We think with the body and in an environment, not only with the brain.

What does it propose?The mind is not just a processor inside the skull: the body, action and the environment are part of how we think.
What does it study?The relationship between perception and action, the role of gestures, tool use and how the environment helps us think.
How does it study it?Experiments on perception and movement, studies with robots, gesture analysis and fieldwork in real situations.
Who took part?James J. Gibson (ecological psychology), Francisco Varela, Evan Thompson and Eleanor Rosch (The Embodied Mind, 1991), George Lakoff and Mark Johnson, Andy Clark, Lawrence Barsalou.
What remains?The idea that gestures, objects and surroundings support thinking, with applications in education, design and robotics.
What is debated?Some striking effects, such as holding a warm drink making us warmer towards others, did not replicate. How far the idea reaches is debated.

Context

Classical cognitive psychology pictured the mind as a program that manipulates symbols, independent of the body running it. From the 1980s several voices questioned this. James J. Gibson had already proposed that we perceive "affordances", that is, possibilities for action: a chair is seen as something to sit on.

In 1991 the Chilean biologist Francisco Varela, the philosopher Evan Thompson and the psychologist Eleanor Rosch published The Embodied Mind, which brought together cognitive science, phenomenology and meditation. People often speak of "4E" cognition: embodied, embedded, enactive and extended.

Main ideas

  • Perception for action: we see the world in terms of what we can do in it.
  • Gestures: children who gesture while explaining a maths problem learn more, according to Susan Goldin-Meadow's studies.
  • Bodily metaphors: Lakoff and Johnson pointed out that we talk about abstract ideas in bodily terms ("being on top", "moving forward").
  • Extended mind: in 1998 Andy Clark and David Chalmers proposed that a notebook or a phone can be part of the process of remembering.

Debate

The approach has been fruitful, but some popular "embodied cognition" experiments failed to replicate. The moderate version, that the body influences thinking, is widely supported. The radical version, that mental representations are not needed, is still debated.

Applications

In education, using manipulable objects and gestures helps children learn maths in primary school, provided the link between object and concept is clear. In robotics, Rodney Brooks built robots in the 1980s that moved effectively without an internal model of the world, reacting directly to their surroundings. In design, Gibson's idea of affordance, popularised by Donald Norman, explains why a good handle "tells" you whether to push or pull.

The body and emotion

Interoception, the perception of the body's internal signals such as heartbeat or breathing, is a growing research topic. Its relationship with anxiety is being studied, as anxiety often involves interpreting normal bodily sensations as dangerous.

The rubber hand

In 1998, Matthew Botvinick and Jonathan Cohen published a striking illusion in Nature. A person rests their hand on a table, hidden behind a screen, and sees a rubber hand in front of them. If someone strokes the real hand and the rubber one with a brush at the same time, after a few minutes many people feel that the rubber hand is theirs, and even flinch if someone threatens it with a hammer. The illusion shows that the sense that our body is ours is built by combining sight, touch and position, and it is now used to study pain and prosthetics.

Mirror neurons: enthusiasm and nuance

In the early 1990s, Giacomo Rizzolatti's team in Parma discovered neurons in monkeys that fired both when grasping an object and when watching another do so. They called them mirror neurons, and for years they were presented as the basis of empathy, imitation, language and even as the key to autism. The neuroscientist Gregory Hickok criticised these extrapolations in 2014: the neurons exist and are interesting, but understanding an action does not seem to depend only on simulating it. It is a good example of how a real finding can be inflated.

The symbol grounding problem

In 1990, Stevan Harnad posed the symbol grounding problem: if a word is defined only by other words, as in a dictionary, how does it come to mean anything? For embodied cognition, meaning is grounded in sensory and motor experience: we understand "grasp" because we have grasped things. The debate has returned forcefully with large language models, which learn only from text and still handle language with great fluency. Whether that amounts to understanding is one of the most interesting open questions in the field.

A school's historical importance and the current scientific support for its ideas are different things: we explain them separately.
